hints: Look carefully at the time axis. When is antigen Y first present in the body? Any response to Y can only start after that arrow.
Remember how a first encounter looks compared to a memory response. A primary response is slower, lower and smaller, while a secondary response is faster, higher and larger because of memory cells.
walkthrough:
**Find when Y can be recognised**

Think like the immune system. At the first arrow only antigen X is injected, so Y is still unknown. Any curve that starts at the first arrow must be anti-X, not anti-Y.

That immediately rules out the two curves starting on the left.

**Recall primary versus secondary shapes**

A primary response happens on first meeting with an antigen. There are no memory cells yet, so clonal selection and expansion take time. The curve is slow to rise, low and short lived.

A secondary response happens on second meeting. Memory B cells respond at once, so the curve is fast to rise, much higher and longer lasting.

**Apply this to the second injection**

At the second arrow both X and Y are injected together. For X this is the second meeting, so expect a tall, fast secondary curve. That is curve B.

For Y this is the very first meeting, so expect a small, slow primary curve starting at the same time. That is curve C.

options.A: Starts after the first injection when only X was present, so it cannot be an anti-Y antibody. It is also tall and fast, not the low primary shape.
options.B: Starts after the second injection but is tall, fast and large. This is the classic secondary memory response, so it is anti-X, not the new primary to Y.
options.C: Starts only after the second injection when Y is first seen, and it is low, slow and small. This perfectly matches a primary response to the new antigen Y.
options.D: Starts after the first injection before Y has ever entered the body, so it cannot involve Y. It is the low primary response to X.
